Stratified means organized or divided into distinct layers or levels, where each layer is separate from the others, sits either above or below them, and is meaningfully different from them. Think of it as a structured stack — not a random pile, but a deliberate arrangement where every layer has its own identity and position.

The word is the adjective form of "stratify," and the noun for a single layer is stratum (plural: strata). When you see "stratified," your mind should immediately picture a clear, ordered, layered structure.

A key idea: in a stratified system, the layers don't freely blend into one another. They stay distinct and separate. This separateness is what makes something stratified rather than just mixed or uniform.
The concept in different areas of life

This is perhaps the most visually obvious use. Stratified rock (also called sedimentary rock) is formed when layers of material — sand, mud, minerals — settle on top of each other over thousands of years. Each layer represents a different period of time. When you see a cliff face with visible horizontal bands of different colors and textures, you're looking at stratified rock. Scientists can read Earth's history directly from those layers. Similarly, soil is often stratified — different layers of topsoil, clay, and rock sit in a fixed order beneath your feet.

The atmosphere is also stratified. It has distinct layers — the troposphere (where weather happens), the stratosphere above it, the mesosphere above that, and so on. Each has its own temperature range, pressure, and composition, and they don't freely mix with one another.

This is one of the most important and widely discussed uses of the word. A stratified society is one that is divided into distinct social layers — classes or ranks — typically based on wealth, power, birth, or status. The upper class, middle class, and lower class are classic strata. The crucial feature of a stratified society is not just that differences exist, but that the layers are relatively rigid — people born into one stratum typically stay in it, and movement between layers is difficult.

Ancient feudal societies, where kings sat at the top, nobles in the middle, and serfs at the bottom, were deeply stratified. India's historic caste system is another well-known example — a rigidly stratified society where your social position was determined entirely by birth. Even modern societies are described as more or less stratified depending on how easy or hard it is to move between economic classes.

When someone calls a workplace, an institution, or a culture "stratified," they mean it has clear, rigid ranks with significant separation between them.

Researchers often use the phrase stratified sampling. When studying a large population, they divide that population into subgroups — or strata — based on a shared characteristic (age group, income level, region, gender, etc.). They then sample from each stratum separately. This guarantees that every layer of the population is represented in the study, instead of leaving it to chance. A study about healthcare habits, for example, might stratify its sample by age group — elderly, middle-aged, young adults, teenagers — and collect data from each group independently.

In biology, "stratified" commonly describes certain types of tissue. Stratified epithelium refers to tissue made up of multiple layers of cells stacked on top of each other. Your skin is a classic example — it has several distinct layers of cells, each with a different role. This is contrasted with simple epithelium, which has just one layer.
The thread that connects every use

No matter the context — geology, society, atmosphere, or biology — "stratified" always points to the same two ideas working together: layers and meaningful separation. Wherever you see this word, something has been divided into a ranked, ordered structure where the divisions are real and the layers don't just blur into each other.
An important nuance: stratified vs. merely "layered"

"Layered" is a broader, more neutral word — it simply means having layers. "Stratified" is stronger and more specific. It implies that the layers are defined, ordered, and — especially in social contexts — resistant to change. A lasagna is layered. A society with entrenched class divisions is stratified. The difference is in how fixed, structured, and hierarchical those layers are.

• "The geologist examined the stratified cliffs and identified five distinct periods of geological history from the separate rock bands."
  • "The country remained deeply stratified even after the revolution — wealth and power had simply shifted to a new upper class."
  • "The lake was thermally stratified, with warm water floating on top and cold water trapped at the bottom."
  • "The researchers used a stratified sample, ensuring that people from every income bracket were equally represented in the survey."
  • "The hospital had a stratified staffing structure: consultants at the top, then registrars, junior doctors, nurses, and administrative staff, each group rarely crossing into the other's domain."

If you had to compress "stratified" into one sentence: it means divided into distinct, ordered, and separate layers or levels, where each layer sits above or below another and maintains its own character. Whether you're talking about rocks, societies, data, or living tissue — that definition holds firm every time.
